projects.title: ValuAI – AI-Powered Property Damage Verification
projects.description: ValuAI is an AI-driven solution designed to ensure transparency in property damage claims for insurance companies. It utilizes multimodal AI to cross-verify claims by analyzing both images and text descriptions, detecting exaggerated repair estimates and hidden damages. This helps insurers validate claims accurately while ensuring homeowners receive fair assessments. We used Gemini Flash 2.0 to process images, and Llama 3 to process text, through the OpenRouter API. I was responsible for developing the entire frontend and integrating it seamlessly with the backend, ensuring a smooth and intuitive user experience. Using React, TypeScript, and Vite, I built an efficient and responsive interface, while connecting it to a Flask-powered backend for real-time damage verification and claim validation.

Imagine accidentally committing an API key… Yeah. That sinking feeling when a secret you were supposed to protect is exposed… it can cost hours, millions, or even your reputation. And it happens to everyone, even the most experienced developers. And the scale of this problem is staggering: in 2023 alone, 12.8 million secrets were leaked on public GitHub repos. And less than 20 days ago, 3,325 secrets were compromised in the Ghost Action supply chain attack affecting PyPI, npm, and DockerHub tokens. That’s why Ritwic Verma and I took on the challenge of building ripenv last weekend at HackGT 12, submitting it to the Warp Best Dev Tool Challenge. ripenv is a secure environment manager built to make accidental leaks nearly impossible. .env files are encrypted client-side, keys are wrapped per teammate, and nothing ever leaves your machine in plaintext. ripenv includes both a CLI powered by Google Gemini for natural language management of secrets, and a web interface made using Next.js and Supabase for project-level secret management and teammate collaboration. No secrets touch our servers. No central vault to compromise. No blind trust in a third party. We don’t - and can’t - see your API keys. And if you’d rather keep everything in-house, ripenv can be deployed internally with the same guarantees. The result? Teams can commit .env files to GitHub, share them across teammates, and push them through CI/CD pipelines - without ever exposing a single secret. Even if the file goes public, it’s just ciphertext. With ripenv, leaking secrets is no longer a risk. Overall, HackGT 12 was an amazing experience. We got to meet incredible people from Warp , Ergo , Visa , and many other companies. A special thanks to Advait Maybhate and Varoon Kodithala for their guidance and invaluable feedback. Huge thanks also to HexLabs, Inc. for hosting the event! No more sending out your API keys over Discord. This past weekend at Hack GT 12, Himansh Chitkara and I built ripenv, a comprehensive solution for managing secrets across development teams. The software industry is facing a growing secrets management crisis. Millions of API keys, tokens, and credentials get exposed every year through public repos, messy pipelines, or supply chain breaches ( https://lnkd.in/gWTPGmb4 ) . We wanted to build something that helps developers and organizations avoid those catastrophic leaks. The idea wasn’t just to lock secrets away, but to do it with a zero-trust, security-first approach while still keeping things simple and smooth for developers. We built a dashboard with Next.js and Supabase for managing team permissions, and a developer-first CLI that understands natural language thanks to Google Gemini. With CI/CD integration for automated secret rotations and a zero-knowledge design, ripenv protects your secrets as seamlessly as Git manages your code. I had the chance to meet some amazing people at HackGT 12, including folks from Warp , Cedar , and several other companies. Special thanks to Advait Maybhate and Varoon Kodithala for their guidance and insights. 🚀 Exciting news from Hack GT 11!🚀 I'm thrilled to share that my team— Cheng-Yuan Li , David Gu , Ritwic Verma , and I—won Best Overall Implementation of MongoDB sponsored by MLH! 🎉 Over an intense 36-hour coding marathon, we developed Med-Ease: An AI-Assisted Diagnostic Workflow, a web app designed to streamline the documentation process for doctors and nurses, letting them focus more on patient care. I worked on the retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) tool, leveraging MongoDB's vector search capabilities to store collections, and using a HuggingFace dataset to train the LLM embeddings. It was both a challenge and a rewarding learning experience! 😁 I couldn't have asked for a better team—we seamlessly collaborated (with minimal merge conflicts 😅). Thanks to Cheng-Yuan, David, and Ritwic for their hard work, and to MLH, Ryan Lay , and the HexLabs, Inc. team for organizing such an incredible event! Key takeaways from Hack GT 11: 💡 Attend workshops: We hit almost every workshop, and each one left us with something valuable. 🤔 Stay focused on the goal: Building a project with a meaningful purpose—like helping healthcare workers—kept us motivated and on track. 😴 Sleep matters: A few hours of rest made all the difference in our productivity and creativity. Check out our project here: https://lnkd.in/dCgjgreb #HackGT11 #AI #MongoDB #Teamwork #Hackathon #HealthcareTech ...more ...more

Summer, in three parts I was recently invited to Jane Street 's Mystery Planet and our team ( Karen Gao , Keshav Shylesh and me) placed third! The premise is that your ship has crash-landed on an alien world and you have a few hours to solve math puzzles for resources and then trade them with other teams way off it. Move too slow and what you want is gone. Move too fast and you've given away it for too little. A few hours of that, taught me so much about how traders actually think and operate in real life On the Hackathons and Projects Side, If you've ever lost half a day of code or GPU time to an out-of-memory error at step 40,000, this one's for you. At the Weights & Biases hackathon we ( Sasha Krigel ) built a multi-agent orchastration which reads your code and changes, tracks memory (RSS, memory usage etc.) and resource usage while the job executes, and surfaces problems early with a concrete fix attached, rather than a stack trace. And finally around all of it, too much tennis and my fellow interns, who made the non-working hours as good as the working ones.
